question: Will a new named storm form in the Atlantic basin between September 17 and September 18, 2026?

calls.reasoning: Climatological 2-day genesis probability around Sep 17-18 is ~24-27% (NHC benchmark dates: 8th named storm ~Sep 9, 9th ~Sep 16, 10th ~Sep 22 => ~0.15 genesis/day). 2026 is running ~0.55-0.6x on named-storm count (5 vs ~7 normal by Sep 4; CSU's 9-storm seasonal total implies ~4 more all season), scaling the prior to ~14%. Conditional evidence cuts further: NHC's Sep 7 8pm EDT outlook shows a completely blank basin with no formation expected through ~Sep 14, CPC's week-3 (Sep 16-22) outlook offers only a 20% contour in a narrow eastern-MDR corridor (~2/7 of that week is our window), and Klotzbach reports record shear plus 'anemic' model development signals through mid-month. Offsetting: the window is 9-11 days out where genesis skill is poor, CPC expects shear to relax further in week 3, African waves emerge every 3-5 days, NHC has named five marginal 40-50 mph systems this year (low naming bar), and subtropical genesis is an off-MDR channel these contours miss. CSU's '97% below average' is an ACE statement and is fully compatible with one weak Fay, so it constrains less than it looks. Landing modestly below the suppression-scaled climatology.

Not depression formation, not invest designation, not a disturbance. A system already at TS strength before Sep 17 does NOT count even if active during the window. Source of record: NHC 2026 Atlantic season summary / TCR page, or NHC advisories & Tropical Weather Outlooks.

STATUS-QUO OUTCOME: No new named storm forms in the window (NO). Nothing is currently active or flagged; the default is continuation of the present pattern.

EVIDENCE — CURRENT STATE
1. NHC Atlantic Tropical Weather Outlook, 2026-09-07 8:00 PM EDT (forecaster Pasch): verbatim 'Tropical cyclone formation is not expected during the next 7 days.' No areas identified anywhere in the North Atlantic, Caribbean, or Gulf. That 7-day horizon ends ~2026-09-14, i.e. ~3 days short of the window opening. (nhc.noaa.gov/gtwo.php, MIATWOAT)
2. Season to date per NHC/Wikipedia (as of 2026-09-04): 5 named storms — Arthur (Jun 17-18), Bertha (Jul 19-24), Cristobal (Aug 12-13), Dolly (Aug 27-28), Edouard (Aug 31-Sep 3). Zero hurricanes, zero majors. Peak intensity across the whole season: 50 mph. Three of the five lasted ~2 days.
3. ACE = 4.4 units as of Sep 4, ~91% below the 1991-2020 date normal; reported as the lowest season-to-date value since 1941. (Insurance Journal / Bloomberg wire, 2026-09-04; weather.com 2026-09-04)
4. Driver per NHC/CSU: robust El Nino, record vertical wind shear (Caribbean July shear reported as highest since records began in 1979), dry air, stable atmosphere. Klotzbach, 2026-09-04: 'We're crushing all sorts of shear records this year. The models are so anemic on storm development coming up in the next 10 days too.' Ten days from Sep 4 = through ~Sep 14.

EVIDENCE — FORWARD LOOK (both directions)
5. CPC Global Tropics Hazards Outlook, issued 2026-09-01, valid Sep 9-22: WEEK 2 (Sep 9-15) — 20% TC formation probability issued between 40W-20W in the eastern MDR, 'where El Nino shearing is expected to remain the lowest.' WEEK 3 (Sep 16-22, contains the window) — 20% probability issued over a BROADER area extending westward beyond 40W, as 'some of the shearing in the MDR is favored to relax further.' Note these are whole-week, at-least-one-formation probabilities over a designated region; the window is 2 of those 7 days.
6. CPC same document on MJO: 'appears to remain active, however its strength and phasing have become increasingly difficult to detect' under the dominant El Nino signal; expected to propagate across the Western Hemisphere and return to the Indian Ocean.
7. CSU/Klotzbach two-week outlook covering the climatological peak: 97% chance activity runs well below average. NOTE this is an ACTIVITY/ACE statement, not a genesis-count statement — a single short-lived 40-45 mph storm contributes near-zero ACE and is compatible with it.
8. Klotzbach also stated he expects the basin will 'eventually at least get one hurricane this year,' and that it would more likely emerge from SUBTROPICAL latitudes than the deep tropics given persistent MDR shear. Subtropical/baroclinic genesis off the US East Coast or in the central subtropical Atlantic is a channel not covered by CPC's MDR contours.
9. Earlier in the season AI-based models (ECMWF AIFS, Google DeepMind) were repeatedly keener on Atlantic development than the physics-based ECMWF/GFS; that divergence was noted in August coverage. Direction of any current AI/physics split for mid-September was not established this run.
10. NHC naming behavior in 2026 has been permissive at the margin: all five storms were brief, weak systems that reached only 40-50 mph, meaning the bar to convert a marginal disturbance into a NAMED storm has been demonstrably low this season.
11. African easterly wave train: waves continue emerging off West Africa on the usual ~3-5 day cadence; the constraint this season has been the environment they encounter (shear, dry air, stability), not wave supply.

BASE RATES (with the class each is computed over)
A. Over ALL Atlantic seasons 1991-2020, unconditional: NHC benchmark climatology places the 8th named storm at ~Sep 9, the 9th at ~Sep 16, the 10th at ~Sep 22 — implying roughly 0.14-0.16 named-storm genesis events per day in the Sep 16-19 stretch. A Poisson over a 2-day window gives ~24-27% for at least one genesis. This is the peak-season unconditional rate.
B. Conditional on the SEASON being well below normal at the peak: 2026 sits at 5 named storms on Sep 4 vs ~7 for the 1991-2020 date normal (ratio ~0.7 on count); CSU's July forecast of 9 named storms for the full season implies ~4 more from Sep 4 onward vs ~7 remaining in a 14-storm normal season (ratio ~0.57). Applying a ~0.55-0.6 rate multiplier to (A) gives roughly 14-16% for the same 2-day window.
C. Conditional on the season's OWN realized rate: 5 named storms over Jun 1 - Sep 4 (96 days) = ~0.052/day season-average; mid-September typically runs well above a season's own average, so the peak-period 2026 rate scales to roughly 0.08-0.10/day, implying ~15-18% over 2 days.
D. Conditional on an EMPTY NHC 7-day outlook in early-to-mid September (a rare state at the climatological peak): no published rate was located for this conditional. The mechanism argued for it is pattern persistence — the large-scale suppression (shear/dry air/unfavorable MJO) that produces a blank peak-season outlook typically persists on a 1-3 week timescale — but this run found no counted historical frequency to attach to it. Treat as reasoning, not a measured rate.
E. Event-in-window check (how many same-length 2-day windows in the last 1-2 years contained an Atlantic named-storm genesis): not computed this run — HU

calls.reasoning: Climatological anchor: a 2-day window on Sept 17-18 (one week past the Sept 10 peak) contains at least one Atlantic genesis in roughly 25-30% of seasons. Three discounts apply. (1) 2026 is running at ~70% of normal named-storm count and ACE 4.4 (slowest start since 1966), with record-strong shear from a strong El Nino. (2) NHC's Sept 7 8PM EDT outlook highlights zero areas and expects no formation through ~Sept 14 — the window opens 3 days past that blank horizon, so YES requires a system not yet on any map. (3) CPC's Global Tropics Hazards Outlook (valid Sept 9-22) covers the window directly and issues only its minimum 20% contour for week 2 in a narrow 40W-20W strip; a 20%/week signal implies single digits for a 2-day slice. Counterweights keep me above that floor: all five 2026 storms were weak one-day wonders, so NHC is naming marginal systems freely; CPC notes MJO propagation into the Western Hemisphere favors genesis during the period; and 10-day-lead skill is poor. No matching market exists — the nearest Polymarket contract (first Atlantic hurricane, Sept 21-25 bucket ~29%, ~$2.2K volume) differs on threshold, scope and window, so it is evidence of a suppressed-but-not-dead regime, not an anchor.

calls.reasoning: Reference class (Atlantic named-storm genesis on Sep 17-18, HURDAT/NHC 1991-2025) gives ~30% for an average season; I count YES years 1993, 2005, 2015, 2019, 2020, 2021 among those recalled. Restricting to quiet/El Nino analog seasons (1982, 1983, 1987, 1991, 1993, 1997, 2006, 2009, 2013, 2014, 2015) drops it to ~2/11 ~ 18%. 2026 is running below even that analog set: 5 weak short-lived storms and zero hurricanes by Sep 4, ACE ~4.4 (91% below normal), described as the quietest Atlantic since 1941, with NOAA's August update cut to 7-13 named storms (~0.7x the 14.4 normal). The most window-specific instrument is CPC's Global Tropics Hazards Outlook issued Sep 1, whose week-3 period (Sep 16-22) carries only a broad 20% contour; a 2-of-7-day slice of a ~20-30% basin-wide weekly probability implies ~8-10%, and the front of that week is the less-favored end since the shear relaxation is forecast to build westward through it. NHC's Sep 7 TWO shows zero disturbances and no formation expected through ~Sep 14, at the climatological peak. Offsetting upside: the window is 9-11 days out, past the TWO horizon, so a system would only need to appear on the board around Sep 12-14; CPC expects the MJO to move into the Western Hemisphere and shear to relax; the African wave train is running late and increasing; and NHC has readily named marginal, short-lived systems all season. Blending the analog rate down toward the CPC-implied figure lands near 11%.

Discount for the observed regime not already in that ratio: record post-July Atlantic shear under a strong El Nino (~90% NOAA odds), a ~14-day genesis drought spanning the climatological peak, an empty NHC TWO through ~Sep 14, and CPC's minimum 20% contour for week 3. calls.reconciliation: The three runs (0.10/0.11/0.12) agreed on the resolution instrument, the status quo (NO), the empty-basin state, and that no matching market exists - so reconciliation turned on their shared discount chain rather than on a spread. Three factual points settled from the dossiers alone (no web access this run). (1) Climatological anchor: Run 3's ~30% comes from a recalled-year count drawn from a 15-16-storm-per-season era its own dossier flags as an upper bound; Run 1's NHC benchmark-date derivation (~24-27%) is the sounder instrument, so ~26%. (2) The dossiers carry two conflicting measures of how far behind 2026 is - ACE 91% below normal vs count only ~2 storms behind. For a genesis-count question the count ratio (~0.7) is the correct multiplier, and CSU's '97% below average' is explicitly an ACE statement (Run 1 flagged this and then did not fully apply it). This is the main reason I sit at the top of the range rather than the middle. (3) Run 2 states CPC 'week 2 (Sept 9-15) contains the window' - factually wrong; the window falls in week 3 (Sep 16-22), which Runs 1 and 3 correctly note carries a BROADER 20% area on westward shear relaxation, so Run 2 applied the more pessimistic contour to the wrong week. Run 3's point that 20% is CPC's lowest drawn contour (a floor, not a point estimate) also corrects a shared downward bias. Unsettled and left carrying its uncertainty: no run - and no check I could make offline - located any published base rate conditioned on 'genesis 10 days after a completely empty peak-season 7-day TWO', so the size of that extra discount remains pure judgment; likewise the MJO evidence is self-cancelling in CPC's own text (propagating into the Western Hemisphere = favorable, but signal 'increasingly difficult to detect' and returning to the Indian Ocean = unfavorable), and I score it neutral rather than picking a side. Market check: all three runs independently found no contract matching this question's terms; Run 3 verified against the live Polymarket weather page that a search snippet claiming a 'Fay' price was false. Run 2's nearest contract (Polymarket first-Atlantic-hurricane Sep 21-25 bucket, ~29%, ~$2.2K volume) differs on threshold, window and scope - evidence, not an anchor, and its thin volume would not support leaning on it even if it matched. Net: 26% x 0.7 = ~18% seasonally adjusted, discounted for record shear and the peak-spanning drought, credited back for the 9-11 day lead, week-3 relaxation, and this season's demonstrably low naming bar - 0.12.
